q: persuasive essay on the ethics of gene editing in humans
ethics of human gene editing essay
should we edit human genes argumentative
a: The ethics of gene editing in humans is one of the most consequential debates of our time. Proponents argue that gene editing could eliminate devastating genetic diseases like Huntington's disease, cystic fibrosis, and sickle cell anemia. The ability to correct disease-causing mutations before birth could spare countless families from suffering and save healthcare systems billions of dollars. Therapeutic gene editing (somatic editing) modifies non-reproductive cells and affects only the individual treated, raising fewer ethical concerns. The real ethical controversy centers on germline editing — modifying sperm, eggs, or embryos. Changes to germline cells would be inherited by all future generations, raising profound questions about consent (future generations cannot consent to genetic modifications that will affect them) and the specter of eugenics (selecting for desired traits). The 2018 case of He Jiankui, who created the first gene-edited babies (twin girls with CRISPR-modified CCR5 genes intended to confer HIV resistance), was widely condemned as unethical and premature. Key ethical concerns include: safety and off-target effects (unintended genetic changes); equity and access (only the wealthy may afford genetic enhancements); the slippery slope from therapy to enhancement; the rights of people with disabilities; and the moral status of embryos. International consensus bans germline editing for reproduction, with over 40 countries having signed treaties prohibiting inheritable genetic modifications. However, scientific capabilities continue to advance faster than regulatory frameworks can adapt. A persuasive argument should weigh the potential to eliminate suffering against the risks of unintended consequences and the fundamental question of whether humans should intentionally alter the human germline.
